Section 2.5 of Lock⁵ turns to relationships between **two quantitative variables**,
displayed in a **scatterplot**: one quantitative variable on the horizontal axis
(usually the **explanatory** variable) and one on the vertical axis (usually the
**response**). When describing a scatterplot we look at the **direction** of the
association (**positive** — above-average values of one variable tend to go with
above-average values of the other; **negative** — above-average with below-average),
the **form** (linear or curved), the **strength** (how closely the points follow
the form), and any **outliers**. The **correlation** $r$ summarizes the strength
and direction of a *linear* relationship on a fixed scale from $-1$ to $+1$: values
near $\pm 1$ mean points hugging a line, values near 0 mean little linear trend.
Key properties: $r$ **does not change when the units of measurement change**, it is
**strongly sensitive to outliers**, $r = 0$ means *no linear* association (a curved
relationship can still have $r = 0$), correlation applies only to **quantitative**
variables, and — as always — **correlation does not imply cause and effect**.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵,
3rd ed., pp. 126–136). Skill Builders 2.186–2.203 match scatterplots to
correlations, predict directions of association, and draw and compute their own;
2.204–2.235 apply the ideas to real studies and Lock5 datasets, several with a
small executable EDA below.


## Exercise 2.194

**Size of a house** and **cost to heat the house**. *(Skill Builder 3: positive or
negative association?)*

- **Positive.** Larger houses have more space to heat, so heating costs rise with
  house size.

## Exercise 2.195

**Distance driven since the last fill-up** and **amount of gas left in the tank**.

- **Negative.** The farther you drive, the more fuel you burn and the less remains
  in the tank.

## Exercise 2.196

**Outside temperature** and **amount of clothes worn**.

- **Negative.** On hot days people wear less; colder days call for more layers.

## Exercise 2.197

**Number of text messages sent** and **number received** on a cell phone.

- **Positive.** Texting is a two-way activity: people who send many messages
  generally receive many as well.

## Exercise 2.198

**Number of people in a square mile** and **number of trees in the square mile**.

- **Negative.** Heavily populated (urban) square miles have their land covered with
  buildings and pavement, leaving fewer trees.

## Exercise 2.199

**Amount of time spent studying** and **grade on the exam**.

- **Positive.** More study time tends to come with better grades (though, as
  always, association alone does not prove that studying *causes* the grade).

## Exercise 2.204

**Light Roast or Dark Roast for Your Coffee?** The longer coffee is roasted, the
less caffeine it has, so an extra-bold dark roast actually has less caffeine than a
light roast.

- **Explanatory variable:** the roasting — how long/darkly the coffee is roasted
  (light roast vs dark roast). **Response variable:** the amount of caffeine in the
  brewed coffee.
- **Negative association.** More roasting goes with *less* caffeine, which is why
  the extra-bold dark roast ends up with less caffeine than the light roast.

## Exercise 2.205

**How Much Potassium Is in Your Spinach?** "Higher amounts of iron in the soil in
which spinach is grown has been associated with lower amounts of potassium in the
leaves."

- **(a)** The two variables are the **amount of iron in the soil** (the explanatory
  variable) and the **amount of potassium in the spinach leaves** (the response) —
  both quantitative.
- **(b)** A **negative** association: higher soil iron goes with lower leaf
  potassium.
- **(c)** **Less than 840 mg.** High soil iron is associated with lower potassium,
  so a cup of spinach grown in iron-rich soil should average below the 840 mg
  baseline.
- **(d)** **Greater than 840 mg** — low soil iron goes with *higher* potassium
  levels. (Remember from Exercise 1.103 that this is an observational association,
  not proof that iron causes the potassium difference.)

## Exercise 2.206

**Reading and the Brain.** More time spent reading was associated with higher
connectivity, while more screen time was associated with lower connectivity.

- **(a)** **(i) Hours reading and connectivity: positive** association.
  **(ii) Hours of screen time and connectivity: negative** association.
- **(b) No.** This was an observational study (Exercise 1.104) — nothing was
  randomly assigned, so confounding variables (parental involvement, income, ...)
  prevent a causal conclusion.

## Exercise 2.207

**Mother's Love, Hippocampus, and Resiliency.** Children with nurturing mothers
had a substantially larger hippocampus, and larger hippocampus area goes with more
resiliency.

- **(a) Positive.** More maternal nurturing is associated with a larger
  hippocampus.
- **(b) Positive.** Larger hippocampus size is associated with greater resiliency.
- **(c)** A randomized experiment would randomly assign some children (families) to
  receive a nurturing-support intervention and others to a control group, then
  measure hippocampus size later. Such an experiment is **not ethical** in humans:
  deliberately withholding nurturing from children in the control group would be
  harmful.
- **(d) Humans: no** — the human evidence is observational, so confounding
  variables prevent a causal conclusion. **Animals (mice): yes** — for the animal
  studies, which were randomized experiments, the causal conclusion is warranted
  *for the animals studied*.

## Exercise 2.208

**Commitment Genes and Cheating Genes.** More cheating by the biological mother
was strongly associated with more cheating by the daughter.

- **Positive association.** Mothers who mated with multiple partners tended to have
  daughters who also mated with multiple partners. (The nest-switching design —
  many chicks raised away from their biological mothers — is what helps separate a
  genetic explanation from an environmental one.)

## Exercise 2.212

**Football, Brain Size, and Cognitive Scores.** Both scatterplots use years
playing football as the explanatory variable; graph (a) shows cognitive percentile
and graph (b) shows left hippocampal volume. The two correlations are $-0.465$ and
$-0.366$.

- **(a)** The two plots look similar, but graph (b) — hippocampal volume — has the
  somewhat tighter linear trend, so **$r=-0.465$ goes with graph (b)** and
  **$r=-0.366$ goes with graph (a)**.
- **(b)** Both correlations are negative: **more years of playing football are
  associated with both a lower cognitive percentile and a smaller left
  hippocampus.** The associations are moderate (not near $\pm 1$) and, since the
  data are observational, they do not by themselves prove that football *causes*
  the differences.

between the husband's age and the wife's age in `MarriageAges`, with the correct
notation.

- **$r = 0.914$.** The correct notation for a correlation computed from sample data
  is **$r$** (as opposed to $\rho$, the correlation of an entire population).

## Exercise 2.217

**What's Wrong with the Statement?** A researcher claims a strong positive
correlation ($r=0.88$) between blood alcohol content (BAC) and the *type* of
alcoholic drink consumed (beer, wine, or hard liquor).

- **Correlation requires two quantitative variables.** Type of drink is
  **categorical** — it has no numerical value to plot or average — so $r$ is simply
  not defined for it. A statistician would instead compare BAC *distributions*
  across the three drink categories (e.g., with side-by-side boxplots or group
  means) and describe the association in those terms.

## Exercise 2.218

**Help for Insomniacs.** Participants were randomly assigned to receive or not
receive cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT); "sleep improvements were strongly
correlated with CBT."

- **CBT is a categorical variable** (received CBT or did not), and correlation is
  only defined between two quantitative variables. The correct description is an
  **association between a categorical explanatory variable and a quantitative (or
  binary) response** — e.g., compare the proportion with sleep improvement between
  the CBT and no-CBT groups. (The randomized design does, however, support a
  causal conclusion — just not a "correlation.")

## Exercise 2.219

**Genetic Diversity and Distance from Africa.** Genetic diversity of 52 human
populations plotted against each population's distance from East Africa (Addis
Ababa) over land (`GeneticDiversity`).

*Data:* `data/ch02/GeneticDiversity.csv` (n = 52), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/GeneticDiversity.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Genetic diversity of 52 populations by overland distance from East Africa
gd = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/GeneticDiversity.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
sns.scatterplot(data=gd, x="Distance", y="GeneticDiversity", hue="Continent",
                s=45, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Distance from East Africa (km)")
ax.set_ylabel("Genetic diversity")
ax.legend(title="Region", fontsize=7, title_fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a)** A **strong, linear, negative** association: the farther a population
  lives from East Africa (by land), the lower its genetic diversity — the
  serial-founder-effect signature of humans migrating out of Africa.
- **(b)** $r = -0.83$ (computed: $-0.835$). The values $\pm 1.22$ are impossible
  ($|r|\le 1$ always), the positive values have the wrong sign, and $-0.14$ is far
  too weak for the tight downward trend.
- **(c)** Both extremes are in the **Americas**: the population with the lowest
  genetic diversity is the **Karitiana (Brazil, America)**, and the population
  farthest from East Africa by land is **also the Karitiana** (about 24,200 km) —
  native Amazonian populations sit at the far bottom right of the plot.
- **(d)** Since greater genetic diversity is thought to aid adaptation,
  populations **closer** to East Africa (Africa itself, at the upper left) appear
  **better suited to adapt to change**, while the farthest, least-diverse
  populations (the Americas) appear least equipped.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({"r": [gd.GeneticDiversity.corr(gd.Distance).round(3)],
              "Lowest-diversity population": [gd.loc[gd.GeneticDiversity.idxmin(), "Population"]],
              "Its continent": [gd.loc[gd.GeneticDiversity.idxmin(), "Continent"]],
              "Farthest population": [gd.loc[gd.Distance.idxmax(), "Population"]],
              "Its distance (km)": [round(gd.Distance.max())]})
```

## Exercise 2.220

**The Happy Planet Index.** Happiness (well-being) vs ecological footprint for 143
countries (`HappyPlanetIndex`).

*Data:* `data/ch02/HappyPlanetIndex.csv` (n = 143), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HappyPlanetIndex.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Happiness and ecological footprint for 143 countries, colored by region
hpi = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/HappyPlanetIndex.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
sns.scatterplot(data=hpi, x="Footprint", y="Happiness", hue="Region",
                palette="colorblind", s=40, ax=ax)
cr = hpi[hpi.Country == "Costa Rica"].iloc[0]
ax.annotate("Costa Rica", (cr.Footprint, cr.Happiness),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, -12), fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Ecological footprint"); ax.set_ylabel("Happiness")
ax.legend(title="Region", fontsize=7, title_fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a) Mostly positive** ($r \approx 0.64$): countries with larger ecological
  footprints tend to have happier, healthier populations — resource use and
  well-being rise together across most of the world.
- **(b)** A country in the **bottom left** uses few resources *and* has low
  well-being — for example **Tanzania (Happiness 2.4, Footprint 1.1)** or Togo:
  impoverished, low-impact countries.
- **(c)** Costa Rica's ecological footprint is about **2.3** — modest resource use
  accompanying the world's highest Happiness score (8.5).
- **(d)** For footprints **between 0 and 6, yes**: larger footprints are strongly
  associated with more happiness ($r \approx 0.62$ within that range). For
  footprints **between 6 and 10, no** — among the highest-impact countries the
  association essentially vanishes ($r \approx 0.04$): beyond a certain level of
  consumption, more resource use buys no additional happiness.
- **(e)** A country in the **upper left** achieves high happiness and health with a
  small ecological footprint — exactly the sustainable well-being Marks advocates
  (Costa Rica is the exemplar).
- **(f)** **Region 1 (Latin America)** stands out: its countries cluster high on
  happiness relative to their footprints — many sit in the upper left half of the
  graph, achieving well-being at modest resource cost.
- **(g)** For countries in the **bottom left**, efforts should focus on raising
  happiness (health, nutrition, well-being) *without* expanding the footprint. For
  countries in the **top right**, efforts should focus on *reducing* the
  ecological footprint while maintaining the happiness they already have.

```{python}
#| echo: false
lo, hi = hpi[hpi.Footprint <= 6], hpi[hpi.Footprint > 6]
pd.DataFrame({"Group": ["All countries", "Footprint 0-6", "Footprint 6-10"],
              "n": [len(hpi), len(lo), len(hi)],
              "r (Happiness vs Footprint)": [round(hpi.Happiness.corr(hpi.Footprint), 3),
                                             round(lo.Happiness.corr(lo.Footprint), 3),
                                             round(hi.Happiness.corr(hi.Footprint), 3)]})
```

  Moon / La Parcela) up to 9.5 (Pumkin Ale) — a range of **7** points.
- **(d)** The highest-average beer was tasted in **2011**: Pumkin Ale (average
  9.5).

## Exercise 2.225

**Is Your Body Language Closed or Open?** People rated as more closed-postured
"had higher levels of stress hormones and said they felt less powerful than those
who had a more open pose."

- **(a)** Three variables, all **quantitative** (given the numerical scales assumed
  in the exercise): the **body-language score** (low = closed, high = open), the
  **stress-hormone level**, and the **feeling-of-power score** (low = less
  powerful, high = more powerful).
- **(b) Negative.** More open body language goes with *lower* stress hormones, so
  body-language score and hormone level are negatively related. If the
  body-language scale were **reversed** (higher = more closed), the *sign of the
  association would flip to positive* — higher reversed score, higher hormones —
  even though the underlying relationship is unchanged.
- **(c) Positive.** More open body language goes with *feeling more powerful*.
  - If **both** scales were reversed, the relationship would **still be positive**
    (reversing both variables leaves the sign of the association unchanged).
  - If **only one** scale were reversed, the sign would **flip to negative**.

## Exercise 2.226

**SAT Scores: Math vs Verbal.** The `StudentSurvey` dataset includes MathSAT and
VerbalSAT scores for 362 students.

*Data:* `data/ch01/StudentSurvey.csv` (n = 362), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/StudentSurvey.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: MathSAT vs VerbalSAT scores for 362 students
ss = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/StudentSurvey.csv")

                ax=ax, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Verbal SAT"); ax.set_ylabel("Math SAT")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a)** A **positive** relationship would imply students who score high on one
  part of the SAT tend to score high on the other (skills travel together). A
  **negative** relationship would imply students strong in math tend to be weak in
  verbal (and vice versa).
- **(b)** A student in each corner of Figure 2.64:
  - **Top left:** high verbal, low math — the verbal whiz.
  - **Top right:** high on both — strong all-around test taker.
  - **Bottom left:** low on both — struggling on both parts.
  - **Bottom right:** high math, low verbal — the math specialist.
- **(c)** The relationship is **moderate, not strong**: there is a clear upward
  trend, but plenty of scatter. SAT subscores are related — a student's two scores
  are far from independent — but knowing one score leaves a lot of uncertainty
  about the other.
- **(d)** $r = 0.445$ — which is exactly the correlation in the data: positive,
  moderate, and far from the extreme options $\pm 0.9$.

```{python}

ss.MathSAT.corr(ss.VerbalSAT).round(3)
```

## Exercise 2.230

**Comparing Global Internet Connections.** Internet speed (Mbps) and hours online
per day for nine countries, from Table 2.36 (`GlobalInternet2019`).

*Data:* printed in the exercise (Table 2.36) — hardcoded here:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Internet speed and hours online per day for nine countries
gi = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Country": ["Switzerland", "United States", "Germany", "Australia",
                 "United Kingdom", "France", "Spain", "Italy", "Brazil"],
     "Speed": [38.85, 32.89, 24.64, 16.36, 22.37, 30.44, 36.06, 17.3, 4.84],
     "Hours": [4.97, 6.52, 4.62, 5.07, 5.77, 4.63, 4.3, 6.07, 9.29]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
sns.scatterplot(data=gi, x="Speed", y="Hours", s=60, color="#4c72b0", ax=ax)
for _, row in gi.iterrows():
    ax.annotate(row.Country, (row.Speed, row.Hours),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4, 4), fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Internet speed (Mbps)"); ax.set_ylabel("Hours online per day")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a)** A **positive** association would mean countries with faster average
  internet have people who spend *more* time online. This could make sense: fast,
  cheap broadband infrastructure goes hand in hand with an online-centered economy
  and culture, so better connectivity accompanies heavier use.
- **(b)** A **negative** association would mean countries with faster internet have
  people who spend *less* time online. That could also make sense: fast connections
  let people finish their online tasks quickly, and in slow-connection countries
  people may linger longer (or the association may reflect some other factor).
- **(c)** The scatterplot shows a **negative** relationship: slower countries tend
  to log more hours. **Brazil** is the clear outlier — by far the slowest speed
  (4.84 Mbps) yet the *most* hours online (9.29/day), placing it far left and far
  above the rest. (The United States is mildly unusual — fast internet with
  near-highest hours — but Brazil is the dominant outlier.)
- **(d)** After removing Brazil, the remaining eight countries still show a
  **negative** relationship, but a much weaker one.
- **(e)** $r = -0.704$ for all nine countries; without Brazil, $r = -0.289$. **Yes
  — the correlation is strongly affected by the outlier**: a single country changes
  $r$ by more than 0.4.
- **(f) No.** These are observational data on nine countries. Confounding variables
  (wealth, infrastructure, work culture, climate and leisure habits) could account
  for the association, so we cannot conclude that a slower connection *causes*
  people to spend more time online.

```{python}
#| echo: false
gi_all = gi.Speed.corr(gi.Hours)
gi_nb = gi[gi.Country != "Brazil"].Speed.corr(gi[gi.Country != "Brazil"].Hours)
pd.DataFrame({"r (all 9 countries)": [round(gi_all, 3)],
              "r (without Brazil)": [round(gi_nb, 3)]})
```

## Exercise 2.231

**Iris Petals.** Petal length and petal width for 150 iris flowers in Fisher's
iris data (`FisherIris`).

*Data:* `data/ch02/FisherIris.csv` (n = 150), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/FisherIris.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Petal width vs petal length for 150 iris flowers
fi = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/FisherIris.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.5))
sns.scatterplot(data=fi, x="PetalLength", y="PetalWidth", s=30,
                color="#4c72b0", ax=ax, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Petal length (mm)"); ax.set_ylabel("Petal width (mm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a) Positive.** Irises with longer petals tend to have wider petals — petal
  dimensions grow together (allometry: body parts scale with one another).
- **(b) Strong.** The main cloud rises tightly along a line from about
  (30 mm, 10 mm) to (70 mm, 25 mm).
- **(c)** About **0.9** (the full Fisher iris data give $r \approx 0.96$).
- **(d)** **No clear outliers** — every point follows the overall positive pattern.
  What stands out instead is a *separate cluster*, not stray points.
- **(e)** A petal of length 30 mm has a width of about **10 mm**.
- **(f)** The plot clearly shows **two groups**: a tight cluster in the bottom left
  (petal lengths of only about 10–20 mm) separated by a gap from the main cloud.
  These are different iris types — the bottom-left cluster is *Iris setosa*, whose
  petals are dramatically smaller than those of versicolor and virginica. The
  scatterplot makes the species difference obvious without knowing the labels.

```{python}
#| echo: false
fi.PetalLength.corr(fi.PetalWidth).round(3)
```

## Exercise 2.232

**Create a Scatterplot.** Draw scatterplots satisfying: (a) $n=10$, $r=1$;
(b) $n=8$, $r=-1$; (c) $n=5$, $r=0$.

- **(a)** Ten points exactly on an *upward*-sloping line — e.g., $(1,1)$ to
  $(10,10)$.
- **(b)** Eight points exactly on a *downward*-sloping line — e.g., $(1,8)$ to
  $(8,1)$.
- **(c)** Five points arranged with no linear trend — e.g., $(1,2), (2,5), (3,3),
  (4,6), (5,4)$, symmetric around a flat middle.

*Data:* constructed to satisfy each condition:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Scatterplots with r = 1, r = -1, and r = 0
a = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.arange(1, 11), "y": np.arange(1, 11, dtype=float)})
b = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.arange(1, 9), "y": np.arange(8, 0, -1, dtype=float)})
c = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "y": [2.0, 5.0, 3.0, 6.0, 4.0]})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7, 2.8))
for axi, d, t in zip(axes, [a, b, c], ["(a) r = 1", "(b) r = -1", "(c) r = 0"]):
    sns.scatterplot(data=d, x="x", y="y", s=45, color="#4c72b0", ax=axi)
    axi.set_title(f"{t} (check: {d.x.corr(d.y):.2f})", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.234

**Do Movies with Larger Budgets Get Higher Audience Ratings?** Budget and
AudienceScore in the `HollywoodMovies` dataset.

*Data:* `data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv` (n = 1295), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HollywoodMovies.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Audience score vs budget for 1295 Hollywood movies
hm = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv")
```

  on the vertical).

  budget of about **$365 million** and an audience rating of **83**.

  on a budget of about **$22 million**.

  noticeably like expensive movies more.

## Exercise 2.235

**Pick a Relationship to Examine.** Dataset: **USStates**; variables: percent of
residents who are **physically active** and percent who are **obese** — two
quantitative variables not analyzed elsewhere in this section.

*Data:* `data/ch02/USStates.csv` (n = 50), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/USStates.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Percent obese vs percent physically active for the 50 US states
us = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/USStates.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
sns.scatterplot(data=us, x="PhysicalActivity", y="Obese", s=45,
                color="#4c72b0", ax=ax)
for name in ["Colorado", "Mississippi", "West Virginia", "Massachusetts"]:
    row = us[us.State == name].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(name, (row.PhysicalActivity, row.Obese),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5, -2), fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Percent physically active"); ax.set_ylabel("Percent obese")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **What we see:** a clear **negative linear** relationship — states where a
  larger share of the population meets physical-activity guidelines have lower
  obesity rates. The association is **strong**: $r = -0.722$ (matching what the
  scatterplot shows).
- **Notable cases:** **Colorado** sits at the favorable end (23.0% obese with
  58.7% active), while **Mississippi** and **West Virginia** anchor the other
  corner (39.5% obese with under 50% active) — the two are candidates for
  outliers on the scatterplot, lying at the extreme of both variables.
- **Correlation vs plot:** the correlation agrees with the visual impression —
  strong, negative, and roughly linear.
- As always, this is an association between states, not proof that inactivity
  *causes* obesity: states differ in income, food environment, climate, and more.

```{python}
#| echo: false
us.PhysicalActivity.corr(us.Obese).round(3)
```
